subject: Archaeology
title: Zheng He's Treasure Fleet
description: A short lesson to help you apply Zheng He's Treasure Fleet.

hook.text: China once had the world's largest navy — ships five times bigger than Columbus's — and then destroyed it.

buildup.text: Admiral Zheng He led seven voyages from 1405 to 1433, reaching Africa with fleets of over 300 ships.

discovery.text: Wreck fragments found in Kenya and Sri Lanka match Chinese ceramics and coins from Zheng He's era.

twist.text: After Zheng He died, the emperor banned ocean voyages and burned the fleet's records. China turned inward for centuries.

climax.text: If the treasure fleet survived, China might have colonized Africa before Europe did.

punchline.text: China had the world's biggest fleet and chose to burn it. Europe sailed instead.

quiz.question: What happened to China's treasure fleet after Zheng He's voyages?
options: It was defeated by a coalition of Southeast Asian navies
The emperor banned ocean voyages and the fleet's records were burned
It continued trading under private merchants for another century

details.summary: Admiral Zheng He led massive Chinese naval expeditions across the Indian Ocean between 1405 and 1433, commanding fleets reportedly including ships over 100 meters long. Underwater searches for these treasure ships continue, though no confirmed wreck of the largest vessels has yet been found.
details.whyItMatters: Zheng He's voyages represent the road not taken — China's brief age of maritime exploration before turning inward. Finding a treasure ship would confirm or revise our understanding of medieval Chinese shipbuilding at its most ambitious scale.
takeaways: Zheng He led seven naval expeditions from 1405 to 1433
His treasure ships may have exceeded 100 meters in length
No confirmed wreck of the largest vessels has been found yet

faq.question: How big were Zheng He's ships really?
faq.answer: Chinese records describe treasure ships up to 120 meters long. Many scholars consider this exaggerated, estimating 60-80 meters as more realistic — still by far the largest wooden ships of their era. Only finding a wreck can settle the debate definitively.

faq.question: Why did China stop its maritime expeditions?
faq.answer: After Zheng He's death in 1433, the Ming court banned ocean voyages, destroyed fleet records, and turned inward. Confucian officials opposed the expense and foreign influence. Within decades, China went from the world's greatest naval power to a state that barely sailed beyond its coast.
